items.readable_text:
Content:
The second-degree Taylor polynomial of a function [MATH: f(x)] about the point [MATH: x=a] is given by

Content:
[MATH: P_2(x) = {\color{blue}f(a)} + {\color{red}f'(a)}(x-a) + {\color{purple}\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)}(x-a)^2.]

Content:
We can use the Taylor polynomial of a function to determine the value of some derivatives of [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x=a.]

Content:
For example, let's consider the following polynomial:

Content:
[MATH: P_2(x)= {\color{blue}-1} + {\color{red}2}(x-1) {\color{purple}\,-\,5}(x-1)^2]

Content:
In this case, we have [MATH: a=1.]

Content:
Now, comparing this polynomial with the general second-degree Taylor polynomial, we see that

Content:
[MATH: f(a)={\color{blue}-1}, \qquad
f'(a)={\color{red}2}, \qquad
\dfrac{1}{2}f''(a)={\color{purple}-5}.]

Content:
In other words,

Content:
- the value of the function [MATH: f(x)] at [MATH: x=1] must be
[MATH: f(1)=-1,]
- the value of the first derivative [MATH: f'(x)] at [MATH: x=1] must be
[MATH: f'(1)=2,]
- the value of the second derivative [MATH: f''(x)] at [MATH: x=1] can be found as follows:
[MATH: \dfrac 1 2 f''(1) = -5 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad f''(1) = -10.]

  • [MATH: f'(-1) >0,] because the slope of the tangent at [MATH: x=-1] is positive. Therefore, the coefficient of the second term in the Taylor polynomial must be positive.

  • [MATH: f''(-1) <0,] because the graph is concave down at [MATH: x=-1.] Therefore, the coefficient of the third term in the Taylor polynomial must be negative.

Only option I meets all of the above criteria.
